title: Vulnerabilities in Systems
description: Common system vulnerabilities and how to prevent them: single points of failure, bypass controls, race conditions, emanations, mobile devices and web-based attacks.

nodes.title: Vulnerabilities in Systems
nodes.description:
Vulnerabilities inevitably arise in complex systems. A single line of code can hold a vulnerability, let alone millions of lines of code and many interconnected systems.
Security professionals must understand where vulnerabilities typically occur and how to design and develop systems to prevent them.
The people involved in design, development, deployment and operations need the right knowledge and training.
Examples: single points of failure, bypass controls, race conditions, emanations, covert channels, aggregation and mobile devices.

children.title: Single Point of Failure
children.description:
A non-redundant part of a larger system. If it fails, the entire system stops working.
Example: a single router or firewall that all traffic to and from the internet must pass through. If it fails, all internet access is lost.

children.title: Redundancy
children.description:
How to prevent single points of failure.
Example: at least two firewalls, configured and interconnected so that the failure of one does not cut the network off from the internet.
You can also have redundancy in software, services, providers and people.

children.title: Bypass Controls
children.description:
Methods intentionally built into a system that allow a security control to be circumvented.
Example: the configuration reset button on the back of a network device. Hold it down with a paper clip or pencil for 5 or 10 seconds and the device resets to factory defaults, forgetting the current administrator password.
They are intentional and created for good reasons, but they add risk by allowing security controls to be circumvented.

children.title: Mitigating Controls
children.description:
Additional controls that reduce the risk of a bypass control to an acceptable level.
Example: physical security, so only authorized people can get near the network device and its reset button.
Mitigating controls can be physical security, enhanced logging and monitoring, segregation of duties and so on. The right one depends on the nature of the bypass control.

children.title: TOCTOU (Race Conditions)
children.description:
An application checks the state of a resource before using it, but the state can change between the check and the use in a way that makes the check invalid. The application may then perform invalid actions.
An attacker tries to slip in and change the resource (a file, a variable, some data in memory) between when it is checked and when it is used.
Full name: Time of Check Time of Use.

children.title: Increase frequency of Re-authentication
children.description:
The answer to look for on the exam: check more often that access is still appropriate. This shrinks the window of time in which an attacker can race in.
There are also more technical defenses, such as exception handling, transactions that provide concurrency controls, and file locks.

children.title: Emanations
children.description:
Radio waves, electrical signals, light, sounds, vibrations and so on that radiate from a system. They can be intercepted to eavesdrop on the system and leak information.
Three major ways to address them: shielding, white noise and control zones.

children.title: Shielding (TEMPEST)
children.description:
Block the emanations from a system so they cannot be detected: Faraday cages for electromagnetic fields, insulation for sound, opaque walls for light.
TEMPEST is a type of shielding developed by the military, designed specifically for devices that emit electromagnetic radiation. Remember: TEMPEST is a method of shielding.

children.title: White Noise
children.description: Broadcast strong random signals that drown out the weak emanations from a secure device.

children.title: Control Zones
children.description: Place high-value systems in physically secured areas, so only authorized people can get near them. An attacker cannot get close enough to detect the emanations.

children.title: Covert Channels
children.description:
Unintentional communication paths that can unintentionally disclose confidential information.
Two major types: storage and timing.
Example: a surge in late-night pizza deliveries to a government building can reveal that a crisis is under way.

children.title: Analysis & Design
children.description: How to address covert channels: carefully examine systems and processes to find these unintentional communication paths, then build in controls to prevent or mitigate them.

children.title: Aggregation & Inference
children.description:
Vulnerabilities that occur when a lot of data is collected and centralized in one place, such as a data warehouse or a big data lake.
The major vulnerability: someone combines pieces of data they are allowed to see and deduces something they are not supposed to know.

children.title: Polyinstantiation
children.description:
Reduces the risk of unauthorized inference. Different versions of the same information or process exist at different classification levels.
A would-be attacker sees only their own version of a process or database row. The other versions, with different information, are invisible to them, which prevents unauthorized inference.

children.title: Mobile Devices
children.description:
A significant vulnerability: they often contain a lot of sensitive information, and they are carried everywhere.
They get left behind in taxis, trains, airplanes and washrooms, and misplaced or stolen devices have caused many privacy breaches.

children.title: Policy, training & procedures
children.description:
Clearly define in writing the acceptable use of mobile devices, in particular requiring that sensitive data is not stored on them, or only in very limited amounts.
Teach employees these rules, and give them step-by-step instructions, so they follow them.

children.title: Remote access security
children.description: Mobile devices are used away from the office. Encrypt their connections back to the corporate network, for example with a VPN, to protect sensitive data in transit.

children.title: End-point security
children.description:
Secure the mobile device itself.
Examples: strong authentication, whole-drive encryption and remote wipe.

children.title: OWASP Mobile Top 10
children.description:
A list, from a well-known open application security community, of the most common security flaws and vulnerabilities in mobile apps. The course uses the 2016 version of the list.
Security professionals must make sure these are addressed in system design, development and operation.
Full name: Open Web Application Security Project.

children.title: M1: Improper Platform Usage
children.description:
The app ignores or misapplies the security features built into the mobile operating system, such as Touch ID, Face ID and Keychain.
Prevent: secure coding and configuration management.

children.title: M2: Insecure Data Storage
children.description:
Sensitive data, such as PII, is kept in unprotected locations on the device. It can be easily accessed if an attacker gets physical access to the device (steals it), or by malware that copies it out and sends it to the attacker.
Prevent: do not keep sensitive data on a mobile device.

children.title: M3: Insecure Communication
children.description:
Most mobile devices talk to a server across the internet, where data in transit can be intercepted and read by an attacker.
Prevent: encrypt data in transit with protocols such as SSL/TLS, and authenticate the server with certificates.

children.title: M4: Insecure Authentication
children.description:
An attacker figures out how the app calls its back-end server, then bypasses the app and sends requests directly to the server, without ever proving who they are.
Prevent: verify the user's identity on the server side, not only in the app.

children.title: M5: Insufficient Cryptography
children.description:
The device uses a weak encryption algorithm, the algorithm is poorly implemented, or both.
Prevent: use good algorithms that have stood the test of time, and implement them properly.

children.title: M6: Insecure Authorization
children.description:
Poor decisions about what functionality a user is allowed to access. This can let an attacker bypass the checks or grant themselves access they are not entitled to.
Prevent: make these permission decisions on the back-end server, not the mobile device. The server must verify that each request from the device is permitted for that user.

children.title: M7: Client Code Quality
children.description:
Poorly written software on the device is vulnerable to common attacks such as memory leaks and buffer overflows, which are exploited with malware or phishing.
Prevent: developers must know and be trained in secure coding practices.

children.title: M8: Code Tampering
children.description:
An attacker changes the app's code or adds new malicious code, so they can do fraudulent things such as stealing identities.
Prevent: the app must be able to detect at runtime if its code has been modified.

children.title: M9: Reverse Engineering
children.description:
An attacker carefully analyzes an app to learn about its back-end servers, find weaknesses in its cryptography, steal intellectual property and so on.
Prevent: use code obfuscation tools. The types of code obfuscation are covered in the first Domain 8 mind map.

children.title: M10: Extraneous Functionality
children.description:
An attacker analyzes an app to find hidden functionality left behind by a developer. It often shows how to gain unauthorized access to back-end servers.
Prevent: remove such leftover features before the app is published, for example through manual code review.

nodes.title: Web-based Vulnerabilities
nodes.description:
A huge and growing share of applications run in a browser and talk to servers over the internet, so the common flaws in them are an important topic on the exam.
Examples: cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery and SQL injection.

children.title: Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
children.description:
Malicious code is planted in otherwise benign and trusted websites, and a visitor's browser downloads and runs the attacker's code.
This lets the attacker run code on victims' machines, for example to exfiltrate data.
Three major types: stored, reflected and DOM.

children.title: Stored (Persistent)
children.description:
The attacker injects code into a vulnerable web application so that it is stored on the server and shown to every later visitor to the page.
Example: instead of a normal comment, the attacker enters JavaScript in a website's comment field. Every later visitor's browser downloads the page with the code embedded, parses it and runs the malicious code.
Persistent: every later user downloads and runs the injected code.

children.title: Reflected (Most common)
children.description:
The malicious code is reflected back to only one specific user.
Example: a phishing email contains a link (URL) with malicious JavaScript in it. The user clicks it and sends the request to the server, the server returns a page that includes the code from the URL, and the user's browser runs it.
Remember: reflected XSS is the most common form of XSS.

children.title: DOM
children.description:
A much more technically complicated form of XSS that happens entirely in the victim's browser, when the page's own client-side script writes attacker data into the page. Rare.
Do not worry about it for the exam.
Full name: Document Object Model.

children.title: Target of Attack: Client
children.description: In XSS, the victim is the user's browser: the attacker's code runs on the user's own machine.

children.title: Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
children.description:
An attacker forces or tricks a user into executing unwanted actions on a web application where the user is currently authenticated.
This lets the attacker execute authorized commands on the server.

children.title: Target of Attack: Server
children.description: In CSRF, the attack passes through the user, and may harm the user, but what is actually attacked is the web application on the back end.

children.title: SQL Injection
children.description:
Web applications use a query language to communicate with their back-end databases, for example to check a username and password, store new data or retrieve data. A user should never be able to directly command and control the database.
In _____, an attacker sends their own database commands to the web server, for example by typing them into a username or password form field. If the web server has not validated the input, it passes the commands on to the database, and the attacker controls the database.
Full name: Structured Query Language.

children.title: Input Validation
children.description:
How to prevent SQL injection: never let database code from a user pass directly to the database. The web server must check everything the user submits, sanitizing it by removing or escaping special characters.
Exam hint: SQL injection and XSS questions can be very technical, with equally technical answers. Boiled down, the answer is almost always that the server checks and sanitizes what the user enters.

children.title: Client Side vs. Server Side
children.description:
Where should input validation happen? Emphatically on the web application's back end, not in the user's browser.
Validation in the browser is trivially easy for an attacker to bypass, so for security, input validation must always be done by the back end.

children.title: Allow Lists vs. Deny Lists
children.description:
Two input validation techniques:
- Permit only specific characters, and block everything else.
- The inverse: block or remove only specific characters, and allow everything else.
The first is more secure, because it is far more restrictive.
You may still see the older terms on the exam: whitelist for the first, blacklist for the second.
